tooltip_popover.content: Theme section under A Story of Numbers

children.name: Evolution of Counting and Landmark Symbols

tooltip_popover.title: Evolution of Counting and Landmark Symbols
tooltip_popover.content: Primitive counting relied on one-to-one matching with fingers, pebbles, and body parts. Civilizations developed landmark numbers to group large quantities without drawing repetitive tallies.
tooltip_popover.example: Roman Numeral System: Landmark symbols I (1), V (5), X (10), L (50), C (100), D (500), M (1000).

tooltip_popover.title: 3.2 Base-n and Place Value Systems
tooltip_popover.content: Theme section under A Story of Numbers

tooltip_popover.title: Comparison of Ancient Base Systems
tooltip_popover.content: Base-n systems select powers of n (n^0, n^1, n^2...) as uniform landmark values. Mesopotamian System: Base 60 (sexagesimal system), preserved today in 60-second minutes and 360-degree circles. Mayan System: Base 20 (vigesimal system). Hindu-Arabic System: Base 10 (decimal system) using positional place value.
tooltip_popover.example: Base-5 Construction Activity ACT-3.1: Grouping 5 ones into a 5-counter, 5 five-counters into a 25-counter. 23 in Base 10 = (43)_5.

children.name: The Hindu Decimal Place Value Revolution and Zero

tooltip_popover.title: The Hindu Decimal Place Value Revolution and Zero
tooltip_popover.content: The Hindu system introduced positional place value where a digit's position determines its magnitude. The symbol '0' served a dual purpose: a placeholder for empty positions and a standalone number. Eliminated the need for infinite new landmark symbols and streamlined arithmetic algorithms.
tooltip_popover.example: Efficiency comparison: In 375, '3' represents 3*10^2, whereas Roman numerals required cumbersome additive/subtractive notation (CCCLXXV).
